studies.title: Abnormalities of frontal-parietal resting-state functional connectivity are related to disease activity in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus.
studies.abstract: Cerebral involvement is common in patients with systemic Lupus erythematosus (SLE) and is characterized by multiple clinical presentations, including cognitive disorders, headaches, and syncope. Several neuroimaging studies have demonstrated cerebral dysfunction during different tasks among SLE patients; however, there have been few studies designed to characterize network alterations or to identify clinical markers capable of reflecting the cerebral involvement in SLE patients. This study was designed to characterize the profile of the cerebral activation area and the functional connectivity of cognitive function in SLE patients by using a task-based and a resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) technique, and to determine whether or not any clinical biomarkers could serve as an indicator of cerebral involvement in this disease. The well-established cognitive function test (Paced Visual Serial Adding Test [PVSAT]) was used. Thirty SLE patients without neuropsychiatric symptoms and 25 age- and gender-matched healthy controls were examined using PVSAT task-based and resting state fMRI. Outside the scanner, the performance of patients and the healthy controls was similar. In the PVSAT task-based fMRI, patients presented significantly expanded areas of activation, and the activated areas exhibited significantly higher functional connectivity strength in patients in the resting state. A positive correlation existed between individual connectivity strength and disease activity scoring. No correlation with cerebral involvement existed for serum markers, such as C3, C4, and anti-dsDNA. Thus, our findings may shed new light on the pathologic mechanism underlying neuropsychiatric SLE, and suggests that disease activity may be a potential effective biomarker reflecting cerebral involvement in SLE.

studies.title: Cardiovascular fitness modulates brain activation associated with spatial learning.
studies.abstract: Aerobic exercise has beneficial effects on cognitive functioning in aging humans, especially on executive functions associated with frontal brain regions. In rodents, exercise has been shown to induce structural and neurophysiological changes especially in the hippocampus and to improve spatial learning. The present study investigated the relationship between cardiovascular fitness, spatial learning and associated patterns of brain activation cross-sectionally and longitudinally in a sample of middle-aged men and women (40-55 years) that took part in a six-month exercise intervention and an additional spatial training. Spatial learning capacities before and after the interventions were measured with a virtual maze task. During this task, participants were repeatedly moved through a virtual town and were instructed to infer the spatial layout of the environment. Brain activations during encoding of the virtual town were assessed with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). The fMRI data revealed that brain activations during successful spatial learning were modulated by the individual fitness level in a neural network, comprising the hippocampus, retrosplenial cortex, cuneus, precuneus, parahippocampal gyrus, caudate nucleus, insula, putamen, and further frontal, temporal, occipital and cingulate regions. Moreover, physical exercising induced changes in cardiovascular fitness that correlated positively with changes in brain activations in the medial frontal gyrus and the cuneus. However, overall spatial learning performance did not vary with cardiovascular fitness. These data suggest that cardiovascular fitness has an impact on brain regions associated with spatial learning in humans and hence, could be a potent intervention to prevent age-related cognitive decline.

studies.title: The use of fMRI to detect neural responses to cognitive interference and planning: evidence for a contribution of task related changes in heart rate?
studies.abstract: fMRI signals during rest are strongly correlated with heart rate variations. These heart rate/fMRI associations may influence the results of brain activation studies, particularly if heart rate is affected by the task. To assess the contribution of task-related heart rate changes on fMRI brain activation related to executive processing, we co-registered the electrocardiogram with fMRI in 91 subjects during an interference task (color-word Stroop) and during a planning task (Tower of London; ToL). We found that both Stroop interference and ToL planning significantly increased heart rate in the scanner and confirmed significant main effects of heart rate regressors on the fMRI signals. Nevertheless, statistical contrasts that test for increased fMRI during Stroop interference and ToL planning were not significantly influenced by inclusion of heart rate regressors. We conclude therefore that fMRI changes associated with heart rate changes do not impact strongly on higher-order fMRI effects in these commonly used executive function tasks, but routinely adding a correction seems prudent.

studies.title: Neural mechanisms mediating association of sympathetic activity and exploration in decision-making.
studies.abstract: The somatic marker hypothesis asserts that decision-making can be guided by feedback of bodily states to the brain. In line with this hypothesis, the present study tested whether sympathetic activity shows an association with a tonic dimension of decision-making, exploratory tendency represented by entropy in information theory, and further examined the neural mechanisms of the association. Twenty participants performed a stochastic reversal learning task that required decision-making in an unstable and uncertain situation. Regional cerebral blood flow was evaluated using (15)O-water positron emission tomography (PET), and cardiovascular indices and concentrations of catecholamine in peripheral blood were also measured, during the task. In reversal learning, increased epinephrine during the task positively correlated with larger entropy, indicating a greater tendency for exploration in decision-making. The increase of epinephrine also correlated with brain activity revealed by PET in the somatosensory cortices, anterior insula, dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, and the dorsal pons. This result is consistent with previously reported brain matrixes of representation of bodily states and interoception. In addition, activity of the anterior insula specifically correlated with entropy, suggesting possible mediation of this brain region between peripheral sympathetic arousal and exploration in decision-making. These findings shed a new light about a role of bodily states in decision-making and underlying neural mechanisms.

studies.title: Brain activity during driving with distraction: an immersive fMRI study.
studies.abstract: Non-invasive measurements of brain activity have an important role to play in understanding driving ability. The current study aimed to identify the neural underpinnings of human driving behavior by visualizing the areas of the brain involved in driving under different levels of demand, such as driving while distracted or making left turns at busy intersections.

studies.title: Neural bases of goal-directed implicit learning.
studies.abstract: Several neuropsychological and neuroimaging studies have been performed to clarify the neural bases of implicit learning, but the question of which brain regions are involved in different forms of implicit learning, including goal-directed learning and habit learning, has not yet been resolved. The present study sought to clarify the mechanisms of goal-directed implicit learning by examining the sugar production factory (SPF) task in conjunction with functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Several brain regions were identified that contribute to learning in the SPF task. Significant learning-related decreases in brain activity were found in the right inferior parietal lobule (IPL), left superior frontal gyrus, right medial frontal gyrus, cerebellar vermis, and left inferior frontal gyrus, while significant learning-related increases in activity were observed in the right inferior frontal gyrus, left precenteral gyrus and, left precuneus. Among these regions, we speculate that the IPL and medial frontal gyrus may specifically be involved in the early stage of goal-directed implicit learning. We also attempted to investigate the role of the striatum, which has a significant role in habit learning, during learning of the SPF task. The results of ROI analysis showed no learning-related change in the activity of the striatum. Although some of the observed learning-related activations in this study have also been previously reported in neuroimaging studies of habit learning, the possibility that specific brain regions involved in goal-direct implicit learning cannot be excluded.

studies.title: Fronto-striatal deficit in Parkinson's disease during semantic event sequencing.
studies.abstract: Studies of Parkinson's disease (PD) suggest that cognitive deficits accompany the classically recognized motor symptoms, and that these cognitive deficits may result from damage to frontal-basal ganglia circuits. PD patients are impaired on ordering events and action components into coherent sequences. In this study, we examined early-stage, nondemented, medicated PD subjects and matched control subjects during a semantic event sequencing task using functional MRI (fMRI). The task required subjects to examine four pictures of meaningful events, determine the correct temporal relationship between each picture, and re-order the pictures into a coherent sequence. There were two main findings. First, we found abnormal activation within the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and the "default" network in the PD group. Distinct areas of the PFC showed both hypoactivation and hyperactivation, whereas the "default" network showed reduced levels of resting activation in PD. Secondly, we observed left caudate hyperactivation in the PD group. The findings are discussed in relationship to how more activation may be compensatory, but does not necessarily mean efficient and correlated brain function.

studies.title: Frontal and parietal networks for conditional motor learning: a positron emission tomography study.
studies.abstract: Studies on nonhuman primates show that the premotor (PM) and prefrontal (PF) areas are necessary for the arbitrary mapping of a set of stimuli onto a set of responses. However, positron emission tomography (PET) measurements of regional cerebral blood flow (rCBF) in human subjects have failed to reveal the predicted rCBF changes during such behavior. We therefore studied rCBF while subjects learned two arbitrary mapping tasks. In the conditional motor task, visual stimuli instructed which of four directions to move a joystick (with the right, dominant hand). In the evaluation task, subjects moved the joystick in a predetermined direction to report whether an arrow pointed in the direction associated with a given stimulus. For both tasks there were three rules: for the nonspatial rule, the pattern within each stimulus determined the correct direction; for the spatial rule, the location of the stimulus did so; and for the fixed-response rule, movement direction was constant regardless of the pattern or its location. For the nonspatial rule, performance of the evaluation task led to a learning-related increase in rCBF in a caudal and ventral part of the premotor cortex (PMvc, area 6), bilaterally, as well as in the putamen and a cingulate motor area (CM, area 24) of the left hemisphere. Decreases in rCBF were observed in several areas: the left ventro-orbital prefrontal cortex (PFv, area 47/12), the left lateral cerebellar hemisphere, and, in the right hemisphere, a dorsal and rostral aspect of PM (PMdr, area 6), dorsal PF (PFd, area 9), and the posterior parietal cortex (area 39/40). During performance of the conditional motor task, there was only a decrease in the parietal area. For the spatial rule, no rCBF change reached significance for the evaluation task, but in the conditional motor task, a ventral and rostral premotor region (PMvr, area 6), the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (PFdl, area 46), and the posterior parietal cortex (area 39/40) showed decreasing rCBF during learning, all in the right hemisphere. These data confirm the predicted rCBF changes in premotor and prefrontal areas during arbitrary mapping tasks and suggest that a broad frontoparietal network may show decreased synaptic activity as arbitrary rules become more familiar.

studies.title: Functional role of the basal ganglia in the planning and execution of actions.
studies.abstract: Recent studies of functional brain imaging have shown the involvement of the basal ganglia in executive processes such as planning and set-shifting. However, the specific contributions of the striatum in those processes remain unknown. This study aimed to test the hypothesis that the caudate nucleus is primarily involved in the preparation of a novel action and not in set-shifting per se.

studies.title: Cerebellar-parietal dysfunctions in multiple sclerosis patients with cerebellar signs.
studies.abstract: Consistent findings have shown that the cerebellum is critically implicated in a broad range of cognitive processes including executive functions. Of note, cerebellar symptoms and a number of cognitive deficits have been widely reported in patients with multiple sclerosis (MS). This study investigated for the first time the role of cerebellar symptoms in modulating the neural networks associated with a cognitive task broadly used in MS patients (Paced Visual Serial Addition Test (PVSAT)). Twelve relapsing-remitting (RR) MS patients with prevalent cerebellar signs and symptoms (RR-MSc), 15 RR-MS patients without cerebellar manifestation (RR-MSnc) and 16 matched-healthy controls were examined during functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). We tested whether the RR-MSc patients displayed abnormal activations within "cognitive" cerebellar regions and other areas typically engaged in working memory and tightly connected with the cerebellum. Despite similar behavioral performances during fMRI, RR-MSc patients displayed, relatively to both RR-MSnc patients and controls, significantly greater responses in the left cerebellar Crus I/Lobule VI. RR-MSc patients also displayed reduced functional connectivity between the left cerebellar Crus I and the right superior parietal lobule (FWE<.05). These results demonstrated that the presence of the cerebellar signs drastically impacts on the neurofunctional networks underlying working memory in MS. The altered communication between the cerebellum and a cortical area implicated in short-term buffering and storage of relevant information, offer new insights into the pathophysiological mechanisms of cognition in MS.

studies.title: Mechanisms of hierarchical reinforcement learning in cortico-striatal circuits 2: evidence from fMRI.
studies.abstract: The frontal lobes may be organized hierarchically such that more rostral frontal regions modulate cognitive control operations in caudal regions. In our companion paper (Frank MJ, Badre D. 2011. Mechanisms of hierarchical reinforcement learning in corticostriatal circuits I: computational analysis. 22:509-526), we provide novel neural circuit and algorithmic models of hierarchical cognitive control in cortico-striatal circuits. Here, we test key model predictions using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Our neural circuit model proposes that contextual representations in rostral frontal cortex influence the striatal gating of contextual representations in caudal frontal cortex. Reinforcement learning operates at each level, such that the system adaptively learns to gate higher order contextual information into rostral regions. Our algorithmic Bayesian "mixture of experts" model captures the key computations of this neural model and provides trial-by-trial estimates of the learner's latent hypothesis states. In the present paper, we used these quantitative estimates to reanalyze fMRI data from a hierarchical reinforcement learning task reported in Badre D, Kayser AS, D'Esposito M. 2010. Frontal cortex and the discovery of abstract action rules. Neuron. 66:315--326. Results validate key predictions of the models and provide evidence for an individual cortico-striatal circuit for reinforcement learning of hierarchical structure at a specific level of policy abstraction. These findings are initially consistent with the proposal that hierarchical control in frontal cortex may emerge from interactions among nested cortico-striatal circuits at different levels of abstraction.

studies.title: Cortical activity in Parkinson's disease during executive processing depends on striatal involvement.
studies.abstract: Patients with idiopathic Parkinson's disease exhibit impairments in executive processes, including planning and set-shifting, even at the early stages of the disease. We have recently developed a new card-sorting task to study the specific role of the caudate nucleus in such executive processes and have shown, using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in young healthy adults, that the caudate nucleus is specifically required when a set-shift must be planned. Here the same fMRI protocol was used to compare the patterns of activation in a group of early-stage Parkinson's disease patients (seven right-handed patients at Hoehn and Yahr stages 1 and 2; mean age 62 years, range 56-70) and matched control subjects. Increased cortical activation was observed in the patients compared with the control group in the condition not specifically requiring the caudate nucleus. On the other hand, decreased cortical activation was observed in the patient group in the condition significantly involving the caudate nucleus. This event-related fMRI study showed a pattern of cortical activation in Parkinson's disease characterized by either reduced or increased activation depending on whether the caudate nucleus was involved or not in the task. This activation pattern included not only the prefrontal regions but also posterior cortical areas in the parietal and prestriate cortex. These findings are not in agreement with the traditional model, which proposes that the nigrostriatal dopamine depletion results in decreased cortical activity. These observations provide further evidence in favour of the hypothesis that not only the nigrostriatal and but also the mesocortical dopaminergic substrate may play a significant role in the cognitive deficits observed in Parkinson's disease.

Inclusion criteria not met/demonstrated: I1 (no clear task-based fMRI/PET reported—appears metabolic imaging in patients), I2 (no problem-solving or reasoning task), I3 (no healthy adult group), I4 (no task-related activation results reported).

Task-based fMRI study of a reasoning/problem-solving task reporting task-related activations in cortical and subcortical regions. Participants are described as subjects with no indication of patient samples, consistent with healthy adult volunteers. Thus it meets I1–I4 and no exclusion criteria are evident.

Excluded because the paper is a coordinate-based meta-analysis (E1). It includes age-matched healthy control subjects and reports task-related brain activation patterns (I3, I4), but is not an original task-based fMRI/PET study (I1) and does not study problem-solving/reasoning tasks in healthy adults (I2).

Study uses task-based fMRI to investigate serial recall/short-term memory order representation, not a problem-solving or reasoning task. (a) Exclusion IDs met: none. (b) Inclusion IDs met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I4 (reports task-related activation). (c) Inclusion IDs not met or not demonstrated: I2 (not a problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (healthy adult sample not explicitly stated).

Excluded because the abstract describes semantic/verbal memory processing, not a problem-solving or reasoning task (I2 not met). Inclusion criteria met: I3 (control/healthy adults implied) and I4 (reports task-related brain activation). I1 (task-based fMRI or PET) is not demonstrated in the abstract. No exclusion criteria clearly met.

This is a non-empirical review of imaging in gestational trophoblastic disease (E1) and does not include healthy adult participants or task-based fMRI/PET problem-solving data (E2). No task-based fMRI/PET study (I1 not met), no human problem-solving/reasoning task (I2 not met), no healthy adult sample (I3 not met), and no task-related brain activation results (I4 not met). Inclusion criteria met: none.

E2 met: study examines metabolic activity in patients with alveolar echinococcosis (disease sample), so no healthy adult sample. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/not demonstrated: I1 (not a task-based PET/fMRI study; FDG-PET for metabolic monitoring), I2 (no problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (no healthy adults), I4 (no task-related activation results reported). Excluded with high confidence based on abstract.

Abstract is a theoretical/review paper proposing ACC evolution; no original human task-based fMRI/PET data or participants performing problem-solving tasks. Exclusion criteria met: E1 (non-empirical review), E2 (no healthy adult sample). Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/demonstrated: I1 (task-based fMRI/PET), I2 (human problem-solving task), I3 (healthy adults), I4 (task-related brain activation results).

Study uses a visuospatial attention task rather than a problem-solving or reasoning task. Exclusion criteria met: none (E1,E2 not met). Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI/PET) and I4 (reports task-related brain activation/deactivation). Inclusion criteria not met or not demonstrated: I2 (not a problem-solving/reasoning task) and I3 (healthy adult sample not clearly reported in abstract).

The abstract reports an event-related fMRI study in humans performing deductive reasoning (problem-solving) tasks, includes healthy adult participants, and reports task-related brain activations during encoding and integration stages. All inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

EXCLUDED because the task was a language/verbal fluency fMRI in epilepsy patients, not a problem-solving or reasoning task. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (healthy adult sample included), I4 (reports task-related activation). Inclusion IDs not met: I2 (participants performing a problem-solving or reasoning task) — not demonstrated.

Excluded (E1, E2): This is a non-empirical review/commentary on immuno-PET imaging without original human data (E1) and it does not report any healthy adult sample (E2). Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not demonstrated: I1 (not a task-based fMRI/PET study of problem solving), I2 (no problem-solving or reasoning task), I3 (no healthy adult group), I4 (no task-related brain activation results).

Study is a task-based fMRI investigation of 3D mental rotation (a problem-solving/reasoning task) in healthy adult men and women, reporting task-related brain activation and hormone correlations. No exclusion criteria met.

Exclusion E2 met: no healthy adult sample (participants are children with TBI and orthopedic injuries). Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion criteria not met: I2 (task is verb generation, not problem-solving/reasoning), I3 (no healthy adult group).

Abstract reports a task-based fMRI study with a visuospatial planning (executive/problem-solving) task, includes a healthy control group, and reports task-related brain activation results (ACC, DLPFC, hippocampus). No exclusion criteria met.

Excluded (E2): single-case clinical report of a 17-year-old with PET findings, not a task-based fMRI/PET study of problem solving in healthy adults. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met: I1 (not task-based problem-solving imaging), I2 (no problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (no healthy adult sample), I4 (no task-related activation results).

Exclusion E2 met: study includes only patients with schizophrenia (no healthy adult sample). Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/not demonstrated: I1 (no evidence this is a task-based PET study), I2 (no problem-solving or reasoning task described), I3 (no healthy adults), I4 (reports regional brain activity correlates with hallucination-proneness, but not task-related activation).

Exclusion met: E2 (no healthy adult sample; study involves patients with carotid artery disease). Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met or not demonstrated: I1 (not a task-based PET/fMRI study—uses acetazolamide pharmacologic challenge), I2 (no problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (no healthy adult group), I4 (reports PET CBF reactivity, not task-related activation).

No exclusion criteria met. Study is a task-based fMRI study (I1), includes healthy adult participants (I3), and reports task-related brain activation results (I4). However, the task is verbal fluency/language generation, not a problem-solving or reasoning task, so I2 is not satisfied.

Excluded because the task is an auditory verbal memory task, not a problem-solving or reasoning task (I2 not met). Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI) and I4 (reports task-related brain activation/connectivity). Inclusion criteria not demonstrated: I2 (problem-solving/reasoning task) not met; I3 (healthy adult sample) not demonstrated in abstract. Exclusion criteria met: none.

Task-based fMRI study in healthy adult musicians performing mental transposition and melody-reversal tasks (cognitive transformation/problem-solving). Reports task-related IPS BOLD activation. All inclusion criteria (I1,I2,I3,I4) are met; no exclusion criteria apply.

Exclusion criteria met: E1 (non-empirical review) and E2 (no healthy adult sample). Inclusion criteria not met: I1 (not a task-based fMRI/PET study), I2 (no problem-solving task), I3 (no healthy adult participants), I4 (no task-related brain activation reported). The abstract describes a review of autism, not original task-based neuroimaging in healthy adults, so exclusion is clear.

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion: I3 met (study includes healthy participants). Not met: I1 not met—uses task-free (resting-state) fMRI rather than task-based fMRI/PET; I2 not met—investigates verbal fluency/language, not a problem-solving/reasoning task; I4 not met—reports resting-state connectivity rather than task-related brain activation.

The task is verbal episodic memory/recognition, not a problem-solving or reasoning task (I2 not met). Abstract reports task-based fMRI (I1) and task-related activations (I4). It does not explicitly state inclusion of healthy adults (I3 not demonstrated). No exclusion criteria met.

Excluded (E2): study uses PET for in-vivo range verification in particle therapy patients, not healthy adults. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/demonstrated: I1 (not a task-based cognitive fMRI/PET study), I2 (no problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (no healthy adult sample), I4 (no task-related brain activation results).

Excluded for E2: no healthy adult sample. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/not demonstrated: I1 (not a task-based fMRI/PET study; uses MRI and FDG-PET for pathology/degeneration), I2 (participants are patients with corticobasal syndrome, no problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (no healthy adult group), I4 (does not report task-related brain activation results).

No exclusion criteria clearly met (E1,E2 not met). Meets I1 (PET task-based study) and I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Does not meet I2: task is verbal memory retention, not problem-solving/reasoning. I3 (healthy adult sample) not demonstrated in abstract. Excluding because key inclusion I2 is not satisfied.

Abstract describes an fMRI study of exact addition/subtraction (a problem-solving/calculation task) with two aphasic patients and 11 healthy age-matched controls, reporting task-related brain activations. All inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

Included for full-text review: the study is a task-based fMRI study, reports task-related brain activation, and includes a healthy adult group (20-year-olds). It is unclear from the abstract whether the mini Ultimatum Game qualifies as a 'problem-solving or reasoning' task (I2), as it is primarily a social decision-making/intentionality task, so full-text review is needed to determine eligibility.

Excluded (E2): study involves adolescents (gender dysphoric and control boys and girls), so it does not include a healthy adult sample. Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion not met/not demonstrated: I2 (task is verbal fluency, not a problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (no healthy adult group).

Task-based fMRI study (n=75) with human participants performing a novel mathematical/problem-solving task, includes an adult group, and reports task-related brain activation (RLPFC and other regions). Meets all inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria are evident from the abstract.

This is a non-human animal study (pet dogs) using a behavioral problem-solving task; it does not use task-based fMRI or PET, includes no human participants, and reports no brain activation results. Exclusion E2 applies. Inclusion criteria I1, I2, I3, and I4 are not met.

Excluded because the study does not investigate problem-solving or reasoning tasks (I2 not met). Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion criteria not met or not demonstrated: I2 (task is visuo-spatial attention reorienting, not problem solving), I3 (healthy adult sample not explicitly stated in abstract). Exclusion criteria met: none.

This is a task-based fMRI study using a non-verbal WCST (a problem-solving/reasoning task) in 14 healthy adult volunteers and reports task-related brain activation results, meeting I1–I4; no exclusion criteria met.

Study uses PET (I1) and investigates cortical language processing (I4) but involves profoundly deaf children with congenital CMV and examines visual language processing rather than problem-solving. No healthy adult sample is included (E2). Thus I2 and I3 are not met.

EXCLUDE: study examines verbal working memory/subvocal rehearsal, not a problem-solving or reasoning task. Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (healthy adults), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion not met: I2 (problem-solving/reasoning task). No exclusion criteria met (E1,E2).

Excluded because E2: no healthy adult sample—study reports fMRI in epilepsy patients undergoing ATL resection. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/demonstrated: I2 (problem-solving/reasoning task in humans), I3 (healthy adult sample), I4 (task-related brain activation results). I1 (task-based fMRI/PET) not clearly demonstrated in abstract.

Study is an fMRI reading task (letter strings), not a problem-solving or reasoning task. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion IDs not met/not demonstrated: I2 (does not involve a problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (healthy adult sample not clearly demonstrated in abstract). Therefore exclude based on failure to meet I2 (and I3 not shown).

No evidence this is a task-based PET/fMRI study of problem solving. Study examines amyloid load with florbetapir PET and cognition in Alzheimer disease; abstract does not report participants performing a problem-solving/reasoning task or task-related activations, and healthy adult sample is not demonstrated. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs not met or not demonstrated: I1, I2, I4 (not met); I3 not demonstrated.

EXCLUDED because the task is a verbal fluency task, not a problem-solving or reasoning task (I2 not met). Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (includes healthy adults), I4 (reports task-related activation). Exclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met: I2 (problem-solving/reasoning task).

Includes task-based fMRI in healthy adults and reports activation (I1, I3, I4 met), but the task is speech-gesture comprehension, not a problem-solving or reasoning task; therefore I2 is not met. No exclusion criteria (E1/E2) apply.

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (includes healthy adult controls), I4 (reports task-related activation/connectivity). Inclusion not met: I2 — the task is a verbal working memory paradigm (executive/WM), not a problem-solving or reasoning task required by the review objective.

Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I4 (reports task-related brain activations). Inclusion IDs not met/not demonstrated: I2 (participants performed a recognition memory task, not a problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (healthy adult sample not explicitly reported).

Study uses an odor recognition memory task, not a problem-solving or reasoning task. Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (healthy adult groups), I4 (task-related brain activation results). Inclusion not met: I2 (problem-solving/reasoning task). No exclusion criteria met (E1,E2 not applicable).

No exclusion criteria met. Excluded because the study investigates memory encoding in older adults, not a problem-solving or reasoning task (fails I2). It is a task-based fMRI study in healthy adults and reports task-related activation (meets I1, I3, I4).

Excluded (E2): study involves patients with brain injury and does not include a healthy adult sample. Inclusion criteria met: []. Inclusion criteria not met/demonstrated: I1 (not a task-based PET/fMRI study; it is a physiological validation), I2 (no problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (no healthy adults), I4 (no task-related brain activation reported).

Excluded because the task is auditory predicative metaphor comprehension, not a problem-solving or reasoning task (I2 not met). The study is task-based fMRI (I1) and reports task-related activations (I4). Healthy adult sample is not clearly demonstrated in the abstract (I3 not demonstrated). No exclusion criteria met.

Abstract reports detection of blood flow changes induced by cognitive demands and mentions cross-validation with fMRI, but it does not specify a problem-solving/reasoning task or explicitly state inclusion of healthy adult participants or that fMRI was task-based. Information is insufficient to confirm I1–I3, so include for full-text review.

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (includes healthy adult control group), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion criterion not met: I2 — the task involved processing emotional and disorder-relevant words in social phobia, not a problem-solving or reasoning task. Therefore excluded from a review of problem-solving fMRI/PET studies in healthy adults.

Excluded because the study investigates pronoun resolution/language comprehension, not a problem-solving or reasoning task (I2 not met). The abstract indicates a task-based fMRI study (I1) and reports task-related brain activations (I4). Participant health status/age not specified (I3 not demonstrated). No exclusion criteria are clearly met from the abstract.

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (healthy adult sample), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion criterion not met: I2 (problem-solving or reasoning task) — the tasks are semantic matching, perceptual matching, and speech production, not explicit problem-solving or reasoning. Thus excluded.

EXCLUDE: This is task-based fMRI reporting task-related activations (I1, I4 met) but the tasks are language learning/comprehension, not problem-solving or reasoning (I2 not met). Healthy adult sample is not explicitly stated (I3 not demonstrated). No exclusion criteria met.

Excluded: study investigates phonological/speech-discrimination processing, not a problem-solving or reasoning task (I2 not met). Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion not demonstrated: I2 (problem-solving task absent), I3 (healthy adult sample not explicitly stated). No exclusion criteria clearly met (E1,E2 not applicable).

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (healthy adults), I4 (reports task-related activation). Inclusion criterion not met: I2 — participants performed speech perception/pseudoword tasks, not a problem-solving or reasoning task relevant to the review objective, so the study does not address problem solving.

EXCLUDE: The task is a delay DNMS short-term memory/motor-preparation paradigm, not a problem-solving or reasoning task (I2 not met). Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI) and I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion criteria not demonstrated: I2 (problem-solving/reasoning task) and I3 (healthy adult sample not explicitly stated). No exclusion criteria from the list are met.

Excluded (E2): the abstract reports fMRI in seven conversion paralysis patients and does not include a healthy adult sample. Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI) and I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion not met/not demonstrated: I2 (task is motor imagery, not a problem-solving or reasoning task) and I3 (no healthy adult group reported).

Empirical task-based fMRI study reporting task-related brain activations (I1, I4). Abstract does not clearly indicate that the task is a problem-solving/reasoning task (I2 unclear) nor explicitly state the participant sample are healthy adults (I3 unclear). No exclusion criteria clearly met; include for full-text review to determine I2 and I3.

E1 applies: this paper is a quantitative meta-analysis (no original human participant data). It does report task-related brain activation results via meta-analysis (I4 met). It is not an original task-based fMRI/PET study (I1 not met), does not involve original participants performing problem-solving/reasoning tasks (focuses on switching/Stroop; I2 not met), and does not include an original healthy adult sample (I3 not met).

The task is a working-memory maintenance and recognition task, not a problem-solving or reasoning task (I2 not met). The study meets I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (healthy adult participants), and I4 (reports task-related activation). No exclusion criteria (E1, E2) are met based on the abstract.

E2 met: study involves children with benign epilepsy and does not include a healthy adult sample. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met or not demonstrated: I1 (no clear evidence of task-based fMRI/PET of problem solving), I2 (no problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (no healthy adult group), I4 (task-related activation for problem solving not reported).

E2 met (study does not include a healthy adult sample). Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met: I1 (not a task-based fMRI/PET study), I2 (no problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (no healthy adult group reported), I4 (no task-related brain activation results reported). The study is a PiB-PET clinical imaging study of corticobasal syndrome patients.

Included for full-text review: this is a task-based fMRI study reporting task-related activations (I1, I4). It examines incongruity detection/resolution—a cognitive process akin to problem solving/reasoning—but the abstract does not explicitly state a problem-solving task nor explicitly confirm healthy adult participants (I2 and I3 unclear). Full text needed to confirm eligibility.

Excluded because E2: study does not include a healthy adult sample. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met: I1 (PET was for receptor binding, not task-based), I2 (no problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (participants were depressed outpatients, not healthy adults), I4 (no task-related brain activation results reported).

Exclusion E2 met: study includes only patients with laryngeal/hypopharyngeal carcinoma, no healthy adult sample. This is a diagnostic/resting FDG-PET in cancer patients, not a task-based PET/fMRI study of problem solving. Inclusion criteria I1-I4 are not met or not demonstrated (I1: task-based PET/fMRI; I2: problem-solving task; I3: healthy adults; I4: task-related brain activation).

Study is a task-based fMRI of auditory selective attention, not a problem-solving or reasoning task. Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion not met/not demonstrated: I2 (participants not performing a problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (healthy adult sample not explicitly reported). Exclusion criteria: none clearly met.

EXCLUDED because the task is visual search/attention, not a problem-solving or reasoning task. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (healthy adult participants), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion criteria not met: I2 (participants performing a problem-solving or reasoning task). No exclusion criteria met (E1, E2).

Task-based fMRI study of relational reasoning with healthy participants aged 11–30; reports task-related brain activation and effective connectivity. Includes adult participants within the sample (up to age 30). Meets all inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria are met based on the abstract.

E2 met: study uses phantoms and point-source measurements, not human participants. It is not a task-based PET/fMRI study of problem solving and does not report task-related brain activation. Inclusion met: none. Inclusion not met: I1, I2, I3, I4.

The study is a PET task examining associative memory encoding and retrieval, not a problem-solving or reasoning task; thus it fails inclusion criterion I2. It meets I1 (task-based PET), I3 (healthy adult participants), and I4 (reports task-related brain activation). No exclusion criteria apply.

Excluded (E2): study is oncologic dynamic PET of prostate disease, not a task-based neuroimaging study and does not include healthy adults. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met: I1 (not task-based fMRI/PET), I2 (no problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (no healthy adult sample), I4 (no task-related brain activation reported).

Exclusion E2 met: this is an engineering/technical PET detector development study with no human participants or healthy adult sample. No inclusion criteria are met: I1 (not a task-based fMRI/PET study involving human participants performing tasks), I2 (no problem-solving or reasoning task in humans), I3 (no healthy adult group), I4 (no task-related brain activation reported).

This is a PET study measuring cortical AChE activity at rest and correlating with neuropsychological tests; it does not involve a task-based fMRI/PET problem-solving or reasoning task, nor report task-related activation. It includes healthy control adults (I3). Therefore it fails I1, I2, and I4 and should be excluded.

Study investigates emotional episodic memory retrieval, not a problem-solving or reasoning task (I2 not met). Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based PET study), I4 (reports task-related brain activations). Inclusion criteria not demonstrated: I2 (problem-solving/reasoning), I3 (explicit healthy adult sample not stated). No exclusion criteria clearly met from abstract.

Excluded because the abstract does not describe a problem-solving or reasoning task (I2 not met); it reports PET results for working memory maintenance/manipulation of orientation. Exclusion criteria met: none (E1/E2 not met). Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based PET), I3 (healthy adult participants implied), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion criteria not met: I2 (problem-solving/reasoning task not demonstrated).

Excluded because the task is a 1-back verbal working memory task, not a problem-solving or reasoning task (I2 not met). The study meets I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (includes healthy adults), and I4 (reports task-related activations). No exclusion criteria met (E1,E2 not applicable).

Abstract reports an fMRI task-based study where human participants performed an anagram (problem-solving) task and authors report task-related brain activation (insula, PFC, ACC). No exclusion criteria apply. All inclusion criteria (I1-I4) are satisfied based on abstract information.

Excluded (E2): study is an animal model with no human participants. No inclusion criteria met: I1 (not task-based fMRI/PET), I2 (not a problem-solving/reasoning task), I3 (no healthy adult sample), I4 (no task-related brain activation reported).

EXCLUDED because the abstract describes an fMRI verbal fluency study, not a problem-solving/reasoning task required by the review. Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (includes adults), I4 (reports task-related activation). Inclusion not met: I2 (no evidence the task is a problem-solving or reasoning task). No exclusion criteria clearly met (E1/E2).

Excluded because it does not meet inclusion criteria I1 (not a task-based fMRI or PET study; uses DOT/fNIRS) and I2 (task is risk decision-making, not problem-solving/reasoning). Meets I3 (healthy adult participants) and I4 (reports task-related brain activation). No exclusion criteria met.

Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (healthy adult sample), I4 (reports task-related activations). Inclusion IDs not met: I2 — study does not assess problem-solving or reasoning tasks (uses pain stimulation and verbal fluency/attention tasks). Therefore excluded from this review focused on problem-solving tasks.

Methodological PET study comparing IDIF estimation methods; not task-based and no problem-solving or reasoning task reported. Includes healthy volunteers but reports no task-related activation. Excluded because it does not meet I1, I2, and I4.

Task-based fMRI study of everyday moral reasoning (decision task) with twelve healthy subjects that reports task-related brain activation results. This satisfies I1, I2, I3, and I4; no exclusion criteria are met.

Excluded (E1, E2): methodological modeling paper optimizing tCS; no original task-based fMRI/PET study of problem solving or healthy adult task participants. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/demonstrated: I1 (not a task-based fMRI/PET study), I2 (no problem-solving task), I3 (no healthy adult sample), I4 (no task-related activation results).

Excluded because the task (embedded figures test) is a perceptual/visual-search task and does not meet I2 (problem-solving/reasoning task) for this review. Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (includes healthy adult controls), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Exclusion criteria met: none ([]). Inclusion not met: I2 (problem-solving/reasoning task).

Excluded because the task is phonological verbal fluency (language production), not a problem-solving or reasoning task required by the review. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I3 (healthy adult participants), I4 (reports task-related activations). Inclusion criterion not met: I2 (problem-solving/reasoning task). Excluded: E1 (study is a trial protocol without original human imaging data) and E2 (no healthy adult sample). E2: Sample comprises nicotine-dependent subjects and does not include a healthy adult sample. Inclusion met: I1 (task-based fMRI/PET) and I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion not met/not demonstrated: I2 (problem-solving/reasoning task) and I3 (healthy adults).

Study reports clinical FDG-PET for prognostic imaging in patients with soft tissue sarcomas. Exclusion: no healthy adult sample (E2). No task-based imaging of problem-solving (I1 not met), no problem-solving/reasoning task (I2), no healthy adults (I3), and no task-related brain activation reported (I4).

EXCLUDE: The task involves humor and theory-of-mind processing, not problem-solving or reasoning, so it does not meet inclusion criterion I2. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (task-based fMRI), I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Exclusion E2 met: no evidence of any healthy adult participants or human data; study is methodological on PET system detectability. Inclusion criteria met: none. Excluded (E2): study involves magnetization transfer MRI in non-small-cell lung cancer patients for radiation planning; it is not a task-based fMRI or PET study (I1 not met), does not involve problem-solving or reasoning tasks (I2 not met), does not include healthy adult participants (I3 not met), and does not report task-related brain activation (I4 not met). No inclusion criteria met.

Title/abstract indicate a task-based fMRI study of problem-solving in humans, fulfilling I1 and I2. The abstract does not specify whether a healthy adult group was included (I3) or explicitly report task-related activation results (I4). Insufficient information to confirm I3/I4, so include for full-text review.

Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I1 (task-based fMRI used) and I4 (reports task-related brain activation). Inclusion IDs not met or not demonstrated: I2 (NOT a problem-solving/reasoning task; focuses on visual processing) and I3 (healthy adult sample not demonstrated in abstract). Therefore excluded.

This is a task-based fMRI study examining visuospatial planning (a problem-solving task) and emotional encoding, includes a healthy control group (n=31), and reports task-related brain activation. All inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply based on the abstract.

E2 met: study is a clinical case report with no healthy adult sample. Does not meet any inclusion criteria: not a task-based fMRI/PET study (I1), participants did not perform problem-solving tasks (I2), no healthy adult group (I3), and no task-related brain activation results reported (I4).

Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I3 (includes elderly healthy control group). fulltext_screening_results.reason: This is a task-based fMRI study in healthy adults that investigates logical reasoning/contradiction identification—a goal-directed cognitive task requiring participants to determine whether a conclusion contradicts a premise (i.e., a problem-solving judgment). The study reports whole-brain, group-level random-effects fMRI analyses, provides stereotactic coordinates in MNI space for task-related BOLD activation, and includes voxelwise results presented in figures/tables with statistical thresholds. Behavioral and BOLD contrasts are reported and BOLD analyses are explicitly described. The full article text (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is present. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not patient-group comparisons only, includes healthy-group task effects, and is empirical). Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the review.

This is an empirical, task-based fMRI study of relational reasoning (Raven’s Progressive Matrices adaptation), which qualifies as a problem-solving task (goal-directed identification and execution of rules to infer a missing matrix element). The study includes healthy adult participants (18-25 years) and reports whole-brain analyses (FIR, whole-brain two-sample t-tests, group-level contrasts) and adult group activation patterns. Data were normalized to MNI space and the manuscript references coordinate-containing results (Supplementary Table, figures), satisfying stereotactic reporting. BOLD fMRI analyses are explicitly reported. Voxelwise/whole-brain results are presented in figures/tables/supplementary materials. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only; empirical with healthy adult task effects). Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion; core content appears complete.

This article is a methodological/review paper summarizing multiple prior neuroimaging studies of insight rather than reporting a original, single task-based fMRI/PET experiment with whole-brain stereotactic coordinate results. It does not present group-level whole-brain analyses with tables of Talairach/MNI coordinates or explicit BOLD/rCBF statistical maps in the text provided. Therefore it does not meet the meta-analysis inclusion requirements. Exclusion: E6 (non-empirical/methods/review without original human coordinate data). Inclusion criteria: none satisfied. Specifically, I5 is not met because this paper is not an original task-based fMRI/PET report; I6 is not met because no whole-brain group-level effects with coordinates are presented; I7 is not met because stereotactic coordinates are not reported for results in this paper; I8 is not met because the paper does not present its own BOLD or rCBF analyses. Full text appears complete (methods/review content present), so fulltext_incomplete=false.

This is a task-based fMRI empirical study of abstract reasoning (a form of problem solving) that meets the review definitions: (1) the abstract reasoning task requires goal-directed solution of novel sequences and higher-order planning/relational operations, satisfying I5; (2) it reports whole-brain, group-level effects including a one-sample (controls) and between-group analyses (I6); (3) stereotactic coordinates are provided in MNI space for activations (I7); (4) results are from BOLD fMRI (I8); (5) voxelwise results/coordinates are reported in tables and figures (I9). The full text (introduction, methods, results, discussion, references) is present. No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) are met. Therefore include.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study in healthy adult participants using a pattern-discovery (inductive reasoning) task that meets the definition of problem solving (goal: discover a category; need to infer how to reach it). The study reports group-level whole-brain random-effects analyses using SPM with MNI normalization, FWE-corrected voxelwise results, and BOLD fMRI data. The manuscript indicates voxelwise activation results (domain contrasts, conjunctions) that would be reported in tables/figures (methods describe MNI template and BA/atlas localization). No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not between-group-only, not a review). Full text (intro, methods, results, discussion) is present.

This is a task-based fMRI study of verbal insight problem solving (Chinese ‘chengyu’ riddles) in healthy adult participants. It meets I5 because the task requires a goal-directed problem-solving process (identifying a novel correct answer via constraint relaxation and selection of novel associations). It meets I6: whole-brain, group-level random-effects analyses were performed using SPM (voxelwise thresholds reported). It meets I7: stereotactic peak coordinates are reported (e.g., −60, −42, 0; 48, 15, 24, etc.). It meets I8: BOLD fMRI (EPI-BOLD) analyses are reported. It meets I9: voxelwise results/coordinates are provided in the main text/tables. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only; includes healthy-group task effects). Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present).

This paper is a whole-brain task-based fMRI study reporting stereotactic coordinates and BOLD results (meets I7, I8) and provides voxelwise results in text/figures (meets I9). However, it does not meet the review’s focus on problem-solving in healthy adults (I5): the tasks are verbal fluency and mental rotation, which are cognitive but not clearly defined here as problem-solving tasks per the review definition. Critically, the study population includes clinical (Asperger Syndrome) and healthy control groups and the reported whole-brain group-level results are primarily contrasts involving the clinical group (diagnosis and diagnosis-by-sex interactions); there are no standalone whole-brain task activation results reported for a healthy adult group alone. Thus it violates exclusion criterion E5 (includes only between-group contrasts / does not provide healthy-group task effects). Full text appears complete. Inclusion criteria met: I7, I8, I9. Inclusion criteria not met: I5, I6. Exclusion criterion met: E5.

This is an fMRI study of three-term relational (logical) reasoning in healthy adults and uses whole-brain, group-level BOLD analyses, but the provided full text does not report stereotactic coordinates (Talairach/MNI) for task-related activations in the text given. Inclusion criteria met: I5 (task-based fMRI of a logical problem-solving task), I6 (whole-brain, group-level analysis), I8 (BOLD analysis reported), I9 (main text indicates voxelwise results/tables/figures are available). Inclusion criterion not met: I7 (no stereotactic coordinates reported in the provided full text). No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. Full article content (intro, methods, results, discussion) is present in the provided text, so fulltext_incomplete=false.

This study examines false-belief (Theory of Mind) reasoning and response inhibition (Go/No-go) using task-based fMRI in healthy adults. However, it does not investigate a problem-solving task as defined by the review (i.e., a task requiring goal-directed planning/sequencing or operations to arrive at a novel solution). Therefore inclusion criterion I5 is not met. Inclusion criteria I6 (whole-brain, group-level fMRI analysis) and I8 (BOLD fMRI analysis) are satisfied. It is not possible to confirm from the provided text whether stereotactic coordinates are reported explicitly (I7) or whether voxelwise results are provided in tables/figures (I9), so these cannot be confirmed as met. No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion present). Hence the study is excluded because it does not study problem-solving per the meta-analysis definition.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study in healthy adults (n=12) that examines relational reasoning (a problem-solving task involving goal-directed inference and manipulation of representations). The paper reports group-level whole-brain analyses using SPM99 with cluster-level inference across the whole brain, provides stereotactic coordinates in Talairach space (e.g., precuneus x=0,y=-62,z=36), and reports task-related BOLD activation contrasts (reasoning vs. rest, maintenance vs. rest, reasoning vs. maintenance, etc.). Voxelwise results and coordinates are reported in the text/tables. All inclusion criteria I5,I6,I7,I8,I9 are met; no exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

Although this is an empirical, whole-brain task-based fMRI study in healthy adults that reports BOLD results and stereotactic (Talairach) coordinates, the task is a visuospatial angle-discrimination judgment (ANGLE vs. COLOR). This is a perceptual/decision discrimination task rather than a problem-solving task as defined (having a goal and needing to figure out a way to reach it). Therefore inclusion criterion I5 (problem-solving task) is not met. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This paper reports task-based BOLD fMRI in healthy adults including an arithmetic (serial addition/subtraction) task that meets the review’s problem-solving definition (I5), reports group-level whole-brain activation effects (I6), and uses BOLD fMRI (I8). However, the provided full text does not present stereotactic coordinate results in Talairach or MNI space nor voxelwise coordinate tables/figures; it explicitly refers readers to primary articles for methodological/details/coordinates. Therefore inclusion criteria I7 and I9 are not satisfied. No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) are explicitly met. As I7 (coordinate reporting) is mandatory, the study cannot be included for this meta-analysis.

This is an fMRI study of false belief and counterfactual reasoning in healthy adults that reports whole-brain, group-level BOLD results with stereotactic coordinates (meets I6, I7, I8, I9). However, the tasks are social reasoning (inferring beliefs or alternative outcomes) rather than problem-solving as defined by the review (a goal-directed task requiring planning/sequencing or executing operations to arrive at a solution); therefore it does not meet I5 (problem-solving task). No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. Full text is complete.

The study is a task-based fMRI investigation in healthy adults of visuospatial judgments (angle vs. color discrimination) with concurrent TMS. It meets imaging-related inclusion criteria (whole-brain group fMRI BOLD analyses and task-related results presented in figures/GLM/GCM), but it does not investigate a problem-solving task as defined by the review (no goal-directed multi-step planning, critical-evaluation, or rule-based solution generation; tasks are perceptual discriminations). Also, the provided full text does not include stereotactic coordinate tables (Talairach/MNI) in the excerpt, so I7 is not confirmed. Therefore I5 (problem-solving task) is not met, and I7 (explicit coordinates) is not verifiable from the provided content. Full text appears complete.

This is an empirical task-based BOLD fMRI study in healthy adults that includes mechanical reasoning tasks (physics puzzles and counterfactual predictions) that meet the review’s definition of problem solving (goal-directed reasoning about physical/mechanical principles). The paper reports whole-brain analyses with group-level random-effects results, provides stereotactic peak coordinates in a standardized atlas (711-2B/Talairach-space variant), and presents voxelwise/BOLD results (including tables and figures). No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not patient-group only, includes within-healthy-group task effects, and is empirical). Full text appears complete (includes introduction, methods, results, discussion, and coordinate tables). Therefore the study satisfies I5, I6, I7, I8, and I9 and should be included.

This study is a task-based fMRI investigation of working memory (auditory continuous performance task with interference) in nonpsychotic relatives and controls. Inclusion criteria met: I6 (provides whole-brain, group-level effects in healthy adult individuals) and I8 (reports BOLD fMRI analyses). Inclusion criteria not met: I5 (the task is a working memory/interference task, not a problem-solving task as defined) and I7 (the full text does not report stereotactic coordinates in Talairach or MNI space). No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) are triggered. Full text appears complete and contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion.

This study does not meet the meta-analysis definition of a problem-solving task (I5). The task employed is a Sternberg delayed recognition working memory task, which involves encoding, maintenance, and recognition but does not involve goal-directed problem solving, planning/sequencing to reach a novel solution, or rule-based problem resolution as defined for I5. Inclusion criteria met: I6 (whole-brain, group-level random-effects fMRI analyses in healthy adults), I7 (reports stereotactic coordinates in MNI space, e.g., x=64,y=18,z=32), I8 (reports BOLD fMRI analyses), I9 (voxelwise results reported/available). No exclusion criteria were triggered (exclusion_criteria_applied = []). Full text appears complete (methods, results, discussion present). Therefore excluded because I5 is not satisfied.

This study is an fMRI experiment in healthy adults and reports BOLD task effects (I8 satisfied). However it does not meet key inclusion requirements for this meta-analysis: (a) the tasks are handwriting/copying and a Kanji-grapheme-puzzle that is primarily a visuospatial/letter-reconstruction task and is not clearly defined or justified as a general problem-solving task per the review definition (I5 not met); (b) the functional acquisition covered only six axial slices (parietal to inferior frontal gyrus) rather than whole-brain coverage and analyses were slice-based, so it does not provide a whole-brain group-level analysis as required (I6 not met); (c) the manuscript does not report stereotactic coordinates in Talairach or MNI space (I7 not met). No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) are directly triggered by the full text provided. Full text appears complete.

This study is an empirical, task-based fMRI investigation of numerical inductive reasoning (a form of problem solving: identifying a rule and computing the next item), performed in healthy adult participants (young and elderly). It reports whole-brain, voxelwise group-level analyses using SPM8, BOLD fMRI results, and stereotactic coordinates in MNI space (supplementary tables/figures). The full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion. Therefore all inclusion criteria I5, I6, I7, I8, and I9 are met, and no exclusion criteria apply.

The study is an event-related fMRI investigation of angle discrimination (visuospatial perceptual task) in healthy adults. It does include whole-brain group-level analyses and reports BOLD results (satisfying I6 and I8). However, it does not examine a problem-solving task as defined by the review (no evidence of goal-directed problem solving, planning, sequencing of actions, or application of rule-based operations to derive novel solutions) so it fails I5. In the provided full text there are no stereotactic coordinate tables or explicit Talairach/MNI coordinates shown, so I7 is not clearly satisfied from the excerpt. No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. Full text appears complete.

The study is a task-based fMRI investigation of four-term analogical reasoning in healthy adult participants, which qualifies as problem solving (inferring a target D based on an A:B relation and mapping/inference processes). It reports whole-brain group-level analyses normalized to MNI space, presents task-related BOLD activation, and provides stereotactic coordinates (MNI) for activation peaks. Though ROI analyses are used, whole-brain results and coordinates are reported, so it does not meet the ROI-only exclusion. Full article content (introduction, methods, results, discussion) is present. Therefore all inclusion criteria are satisfied (I5, I6, I7, I8, I9) and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is a task-based fMRI study in healthy adults that examines mental arithmetic (addition of four two-digit numbers), which meets the review’s definition of problem solving (goal-directed manipulation and execution of rule-based operations). It reports whole-brain, group-level random-effects voxelwise analyses using MNI space, with BOLD results and coordinate-based activations. The full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not between-group-only, not clinical comparisons, not non-empirical).

This is a task-based fMRI study in healthy adult participants using the Hit-N sequential game (a goal-directed problem-solving task: reach the final position by planning moves). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain random-effects GLM analyses (rfxGLM) and presents voxelwise activation maps and cluster results (including FDR thresholds). Stereotactic coordinates are reported in Talairach space (e.g., VLPFC at 47, 40, 3; insula/striatum coordinates described), and the imaging modality is BOLD fMRI with whole-brain preprocessing and analysis described. Voxelwise results are presented in figures and described in text. Therefore all inclusion criteria I5, I6, I7, I8, and I9 are satisfied. No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. Full text appears complete (includes introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is a task-based, event-related fMRI study of verbal analogical reasoning in healthy adults that meets the review objective. It uses a problem-solving/analogy task requiring goal-directed retrieval, integration, and evaluation (qualifies as problem solving). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses, provides stereotactic coordinates in MNI space (tables/figures), and analyzes BOLD signal (event-related fMRI). No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion, so the record is complete for screening.

This is an empirical, task-based fMRI study in healthy adult participants investigating analogical reasoning. The task requires establishing a goal and deriving the correct response by integrating spatial relations and inhibiting superficial responses, which fits the review's definition of problem solving/critical thinking. The study reports group-level, whole-brain random-effects analyses with multiple-comparison correction, provides stereotactic coordinates in MNI space (e.g., R IFG x=52,y=40,z=10), and analyzes BOLD signal. Voxelwise and ROI results are presented in the main text. The full text includes Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I5, I6, I7, I8, and I9, and no exclusion criteria are met.

This is a task-based, whole-brain BOLD fMRI study in healthy adults that examines rule-based manipulation within working memory. The manipulation trials require subjects to apply prelearned reordering rules to achieve a goal, which fits the review's problem-solving definition (goal-directed, planning/sequencing/rule-based operations to arrive at a correct solution). The study reports group-level, random-effects whole-brain analyses in MNI stereotaxic space, provides voxelwise results and figures/tables, and uses BOLD fMRI contrasts. All required inclusion criteria are satisfied (I5, I6, I7, I8, I9). No exclusion criteria are met. Full text includes introduction, methods, results and discussion and appears complete.

This fMRI study includes an explicit deductive reasoning (logic) localizer task that meets the review's definition of problem-solving (goal-directed deductive inference using rule-based logical operations). It reports group-level whole-brain fMRI analyses in healthy adult participants, with task-related activations reported as stereotactic Talairach coordinates and BOLD-based measures. The full text contains methods, results (including whole-brain contrasts and coordinate tables), and discussion. Therefore it satisfies inclusion criteria I5 (task-based problem-solving/logical task), I6 (whole-brain group-level effects in healthy adults), I7 (stereotactic coordinates reported in Talairach space), I8 (BOLD fMRI analysis), and I9 (voxelwise results presented in tables/figures). No exclusion criteria are met. Full text appears complete.

Although this is a task-based, whole-brain fMRI study in healthy adults reporting BOLD results in Talairach space (and voxelwise results), the experimental task is empathic/emotional state reasoning (inferring causes of facial expressions from four candidate situations). This does not meet the meta-analysis definition of a problem-solving task (I5) which requires goal-directed problem solving involving evaluation, planning/sequencing actions, and executing operations under a rule set to arrive at a (sometimes novel) solution. The present task is an emotion inference/forced-choice matching task rather than planning, sequencing, or rule-based problem solving across domains. Therefore it fails inclusion criterion I5. No exclusion criteria (E3-E6) apply. Full text appears complete.

The study is a task-based fMRI experiment in healthy adult participants performing goal-directed, rule-based mental-operation tasks (numeral addition, spatial marker movement, verbal sequencing). These tasks meet the review’s problem-solving definition (I5). The paper reports whole-brain, group-level random-effects analyses in healthy adults (I6), provides stereotactic coordinates (MNI) for task-related activations (I7), uses BOLD fMRI (I8), and reports voxelwise results/coordinates in the text (I9). No exclusion criteria are met: analyses are not ROI-only, not limited to disease/age/gender comparisons, include within-group task effects for healthy participants, and are empirical. Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion, so content is complete.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study in healthy adult participants (university students) that uses a mental-arithmetic verification task ((a×b)−c=d) that fits the review’s operational definition of problem solving (goal-directed algebraic operations requiring planning/sequencing and rule-based execution). The study reports group-level, whole-brain random-effects GLM analyses on transformed Talairach-space data, uses BOLD fMRI, and provides voxelwise/ROI results in tables/figures (and supplementary materials), satisfying coordinate reporting. Participants are healthy adults and task effects (math>word and cue/task contrasts) are explicitly analyzed. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not non-empirical, includes within-group task effects in healthy subjects). Full text contains Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion, so the full text appears complete for screening purposes.

This is a task-based fMRI study in healthy adults that examines probabilistic reasoning/decision making under uncertainty, which involves formulating competing hypotheses, evaluating evidence, and deciding — meeting the review's problem-solving definition (I5). The study reports BOLD fMRI acquisition and analysis (I8), performs whole-brain voxelwise group-level analyses (fixed-effects across 8 healthy adults) with multiple-comparison correction (I6), and indicates stereotactic coordinate reporting and conversion to Talairach/MNI space (I7). Results and core article sections (introduction, methods, results, discussion) are present in the provided full text, and qualifying voxelwise results are described (I9). No exclusion criteria are met: analyses are whole-brain (not ROI-only), involve healthy-group task effects (not only between-group comparisons), and the paper is empirical. Full text appears complete for screening purposes.

This PET study in healthy adult participants reports whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analyses (SPM99) of task-related rCBF changes, including stereotactic coordinates in standardized space. The complex mental calculation task (2x2-digit multiplications) clearly meets the review’s definition of problem solving (goal-directed arithmetic operations requiring planning/sequencing and rule-based execution). Whole-brain PET rCBF analyses and conjunction/contrast results are reported with coordinates; results are not ROI-only. Full methods, results, and discussion are present in the provided full text. Therefore all inclusion criteria I5, I6, I7, I8 and I9 are met, and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study in healthy adults that directly investigates transitive (logical) reasoning—a form of problem solving under a logical rule set—and includes a number-comparison task. The study used BOLD fMRI, normalized functional images to the Montreal Neurological Institute template, and performed whole-brain random-effects voxelwise analyses (voxel-level P<0.01, cluster-level P<0.05 corrected). Stereotactic coordinates for activations (x,y,z) are reported (MNI space), and voxelwise results are shown in figures and ROI analyses; tables/figures provide the necessary spatial results. Participants were healthy adults (n=15 after exclusions). Therefore all inclusion criteria are met (I5–I9). No exclusion criteria apply (no ROI-only reporting, no patient-group-only contrasts, and this is empirical original human data). Full text is complete.

The task studied is a visuospatial matching task (selecting matching/development figures), not a problem-solving task as defined (planning/sequencing/evaluative critical thinking to reach a solution). Although this is a whole-brain, task-based BOLD fMRI study with group-level effects and voxelwise activation maps, the paper does not report stereotactic coordinates (Talairach/MNI) for task-related increases in the provided full text. Therefore it fails to meet I5 (problem-solving task) and I7 (reports stereotactic coordinates). It does meet I6 and I8 (whole-brain group BOLD fMRI) and I9 (voxelwise results presented in figures), and it does not meet any exclusion criteria. Full text appears complete. Exclusion is based on missing required inclusion criteria.

This is an empirical, task-based fMRI study of problem solving (arithmetic Pyramid and Formula problems) in healthy adult participants (n=20). It includes whole-brain analyses (classification using whole-brain mega-voxels and exploratory whole-brain contrasts), reports group-level effects, and provides stereotactic coordinates (Talairach coordinates cited for HIPS and angular gyrus). The study uses BOLD fMRI and reports voxelwise results (with cluster thresholds and coordinates referenced). All specified inclusion criteria are met (I5, I6, I7, I8, I9). No exclusion criteria apply. Full text appears complete (introduction, methods, results, discussion).

This is a task-based fMRI study of mental arithmetic in healthy adults (meets I5: problem-solving task; meets I8: reports BOLD fMRI). However, the manuscript reports results based on anatomically defined ROI extractions (beta values) and correlations with DTI measures and does not present whole-brain, voxelwise group-level stereotactic coordinate results (no Talairach/MNI coordinate tables or whole-brain activation peaks are provided in the supplied full text). Therefore it fails to meet I6 (at least one whole-brain group-level analysis reported) and I7 (stereotactic coordinate results), and meets exclusion criterion E3 (reports only ROI results). Accordingly the study must be excluded from the meta-analysis.

This study investigated parietal cortex involvement in visuospatial discrimination (angle, colour, conjunction) using task-based fMRI and rTMS. It does not study a problem-solving task as defined in inclusion criterion I5 (goal-directed critical thinking/planning/sequencing to reach a previously unknown solution); instead it uses perceptual/discrimination tasks. The provided full text contains introduction, methods, results, and discussion (fulltext_incomplete=false). Inclusion criteria met: I6 (group-level whole-brain fMRI analysis in healthy adults) and I8 (reports BOLD analyses). Inclusion criteria not met: I5 (task is not problem-solving) and I7 (no stereotactic coordinates reported in the provided text). No exclusion criteria (E3–E6) apply. Therefore the study must be excluded because it fails to meet I5 (and I7 based on the provided text).

This is a task-based fMRI study of clinical reasoning (MCQ diagnostic problem solving) in healthy adult physicians and interns, which meets the review’s problem-solving definition (goal-directed diagnostic decisions). The study reports whole-brain voxelwise analyses with second-level/group effects (random-effects, conjunction and direct group comparisons) and family-wise error cluster correction. Anatomical scans were registered to Talairach space and results are reported with Talairach coordinates (figures/tables referenced). The imaging analysis is BOLD-based fMRI (percent-change-from-mean). Task-related activations are reported in the main text and figures/tables, satisfying coordinate reporting and acceptable presentation formats. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, disease-only, non-empirical) are met.

This is a task-based whole-brain fMRI study in healthy adults that directly investigates reasoning/problem-solving processes. The experimental tasks require goal-directed relational reasoning (choosing the appropriate final scene given an initial scene) and an episodic-memory-based reasoning task, meeting the review’s definition of problem solving (goal, need to determine a way to reach it, selection/manipulation processes).
